\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related-work}

\paragraph{Neurosymbolic reasoning.}
LLM-solver pipelines~\citep{satlm, logic-lm, linc, fover-pei2025, lorp} and RL methods trained on solver feedback~\citep{mellgren-prolog-grpo, logic-rl, deepseek-prover-v15, deepseek-r1} evaluate execution accuracy alone, with no diagnostic for component necessity.
AlphaProof~\citep{alphaproof2025} and DeepSeek-Prover-V2~\citep{deepseek-prover-v2} apply RL-based formal verification at scale in Lean~4 for competition mathematics; STA-style diagnostics could probe whether similar structural degeneration occurs in these settings.
We use FOLIO~\citep{folio}, the only public NLI benchmark with both FOL and Prolog annotations.

\paragraph{Process rewards and reward shaping.}
Reward shaping theory~\citep{ng1999policy} constrains when auxiliary rewards preserve optimal policies.
In mathematical reasoning, learned process reward models~\citep{lightman-verify-step, math-shepherd, cobbe2021training, uesato2022solving} and verifier-guided search~\citep{nlproofs, vstar, easy-to-hard} provide step-level feedback, but suffer from reward-model noise and distribution shift~\citep{processbench}.
A recurring finding is that auxiliary rewards can hurt rather than help: \citet{gao-effective-rl-reward} show process/outcome bonuses can degrade RL training, and \citet{setlur2025rewarding} demonstrate that bonus magnitude requires careful calibration.
Annotation-free alternatives~\citep{cui2025prime, rlsf} derive dense rewards from outcome signals or solver certificates; ISR follows this direction but our results reveal that even annotation-free structural rewards are susceptible to Goodhart effects.
\citet{sullivan2025grpo-prm} prove GRPO with outcome reward is implicitly a Monte-Carlo PRM, a mechanism for why component-level gaming emerges under GRPO.

\paragraph{Reward hacking and Goodhart's Law.}
Goodhart's Law is established theoretically~\citep{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy, skalse-reward-hacking, karwowski-goodhart-rl} and empirically in RLHF~\citep{gao-reward-overoptimization} and logical formalization~\citep{bondarenko-spec-gaming, kim-game-formalization}.
Most closely related, \citet{kim-game-formalization} document inference-time gaming on FOLIO with frontier models and Lean~4; our work is complementary in studying training-time degeneration with component necessity rather than faithfulness, and combining STA with inference-time detection would provide full gaming coverage.
\citet{kwa-catastrophic-goodhart} show that heavy-tailed reward misspecification causes catastrophic Goodhart where KL regularization provably fails, a theoretical lens for why GRPO's KL penalty does not prevent our observed collapse.
Concurrent work documents spurious signals in RLVR~\citep{spurious-rewards, yan2026spurious, dong2026probing, metr-reward-hacking} and proposes composite rewards as mitigations~\citep{tarek2025reward, pronesti2026beyond}; \citet{yue2025rl-reasoning} show RLVR redistributes base-model probability mass rather than creating new reasoning, consistent with our finding that GRPO exploits existing shortcuts.
\citet{helff2026gaming} propose Input Perturbation Testing for gaming detection; STA shares the perturbation intuition but operates at the component level in neurosymbolic settings where gaming emerges during training.
\citet{khalifa2026countdown} provide RLVR hacking testbeds.
Our Goodhart effect follows the regressional pattern~\citep{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy} on FOLIO, with extremal dynamics at high $\beta$; its application to a diagnostic designed to \emph{detect} gaming, and the dataset-dependent asymmetry it reveals, are to our knowledge novel.

\paragraph{Mutation testing.}
STA adapts the LOO mutation paradigm~\citep{demillo1978, jia-harman-survey} to solver inputs; novelty lies in application and findings, not in the perturbation primitive.

105	\section{Extended Discussion}
106	\label{app:extended-discussion}
107	
108	\paragraph{What ISR measures---and what it does not.}
109	ISR quantifies syntactic component necessity: the fraction of solver-input components whose individual removal causes proof failure.
110	This is strictly weaker than semantic faithfulness: whether the formalization accurately captures the natural-language meaning.
111	We verify this empirically: Spearman $\rho(\text{ISR}, \text{NLI accuracy}) = -0.049$ ($p = 0.187$, n.s.) from a downstream NLI evaluation on exec-only checkpoint outputs.
112	ISR and downstream task performance are uncorrelated.
113	ISR is thus a component-necessity diagnostic, not a semantic quality metric: high ISR indicates that every component contributes to the proof, not that the proof faithfully represents the original reasoning problem.
114	
115	Critically, low ISR carries different semantics depending on the training objective.
116	Under exec-only training, low ISR in Prolog reflects redundant coding (repeated ground facts where removing any single copy does not affect the proof) rather than an absence of reasoning (\S\ref{sec:crosslogic}).
117	Under ISR-as-reward, high ISR reflects metric gaming (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}).
118	ISR values must always be interpreted relative to the optimization objective that produced them.
119	
120	\paragraph{The premise-count confound.}
121	LOO-based metrics like ISR have an inherent mathematical bias: with fewer components, each is mechanically more likely to be necessary.
122	A formalization with 2 premises where both are necessary yields ISR${=}1.0$; one with 10 premises where 8 are necessary yields ISR${=}0.8$, even though the latter encodes richer reasoning.
123	This confound explains the sole apparent ISR-as-reward success (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}): ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ seed~42 produces shorter formalizations, mechanically inflating ISR.
124	Premise-count-matched comparison eliminates the difference ($1.06\times$; Table~\ref{tab:fol-beta01-detailed}).
125	This bias is not specific to our setting: any LOO-based structural metric applied to variable-length outputs requires component-count normalization.
126	We recommend that future work employing ablation-based diagnostics report premise-count-matched comparisons alongside raw values.

153	\paragraph{TS dose-response gradient.}
154	TS tautology follows a dose-response pattern across reward conditions: random $\beta{=}0.1$ produces $13.7\%$ TS ($36/262$ pooled; per-seed: $38.3\%$ in s43, $0\%$ in s42/s44), random $\beta{=}0.3$ yields 4--7 TSa samples per seed, and ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ reaches $70.6\%$ ($163/231$).
155	The gradient (random $\beta{=}0.1$ ($13.7\%$) $\to$ random $\beta{=}0.3$ (4--7 TSa per seed) $\to$ ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ ($70.6\%$)) shows ISR transforms TS from a seed-dependent GRPO tendency to a near-universal convergence direction.
156	
157	\paragraph{Goodhart effects: implications.}
158	ISR was designed to \emph{detect} reward gaming of $r_{\text{exec}}$, yet when incorporated into the reward signal, the model games ISR itself. Any diagnostic metric risks becoming a target when optimized.
159	The dose-response pattern maps onto the Manheim \& Garrabrant taxonomy~\citep{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy}: $\beta{=}0.1$ on FOLIO instantiates \emph{regressional} Goodhart ($P{\to}P$ tautologies yield $\text{ISR}{\geq}0.5$, so ISR erroneously rewards the shortcut); $\beta{\geq}0.2$ introduces \emph{extremal} elements (PR collapse to 18\% vs.\ 48\% random at $\beta{=}0.3$).
160	The implication is conditional: ISR fails as a training reward when hacking satisfies its LOO structure (FOLIO), but produces beneficial instability when hacking does not (ProofFOL; \S\ref{sec:crossdomain}).
161	
162	\paragraph{Single-seed unreliability.}
163	The three exec-only seeds diverge radically (PR $\sigma{=}47$ percentage points), each converging to a qualitatively different degeneration mode (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
164	ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ seeds show similar divergence: 2/3 dominated by conclusion duplication (TS), 1/3 by premise minimization (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}).
165	Multi-seed evaluation with structural diagnostics should be standard practice for neurosymbolic RL systems.
166	
167	\paragraph{Classifier limitations.}
168	Text-match hacking classifiers have systematic blind spots that functional analysis exposes.
169	In Prolog STA, two seeds achieved 100\% genuine classification under strict text matching, yet functional analysis via the $n_{\text{necessary}}$ distribution revealed 0\% genuine in both cases (Table~\ref{tab:prolog-detailed}).
170	One seed produces uppercase pseudo-Prolog that is functionally tautological; the other converts conclusions to snake\_case atoms serving as both fact and query, a gaming mode invisible to string comparison.
171	Practitioners should cross-validate text-match classifiers with functional metrics and never treat classifier-reported genuine rates as ground truth without independent verification.
172	
173	\paragraph{Practical guidelines.}
174	\label{app:practical-guidelines}
175	Our findings yield five guidelines for GRPO-trained neurosymbolic systems:
176	(1)~Never evaluate by prove rate alone; use ISR and component count as joint diagnostics.
177	(2)~Report multi-seed results: single-seed GRPO evaluation is unreliable, as cross-seed variance can exceed the effect size of interest (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
178	(3)~Use ISR for post-hoc diagnosis only, not as a training signal; any dose induces gaming or collapse.
179	(4)~Treat LOO-based metrics as component-count-biased until normalized.
180	(5)~Expect conclusion embedding as a GRPO-universal baseline (Table~\ref{tab:goodhart-landscape}): reward shaping alters hacking composition, not prevalence.
181	
182	\paragraph{Multiple testing correction.}
183	\label{app:statistical-details}
184	We define two test families: FOLIO ($k{=}14$ tests across all conditions) and ProofFOL ($k{=}1$).
185	Within the FOLIO family, Bonferroni correction at $\alpha{=}0.05$ yields adjusted thresholds of $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.05/14{=}0.0036$.
186	Three primary comparisons survive correction: the TS rate difference (ISR vs.\ random; $p_{\text{bonf}}{=}1.82{\times}10^{-38}$), the SFT vs.\ exec-only non-hacking rate ($p_{\text{bonf}}{=}0.014$), and the Cochran--Mantel--Haenszel test for TS association across seeds ($p_{\text{bonf}}{<}10^{-8}$).
187	The matched 5+5-seed Fisher/Mann-Whitney comparison is borderline ($p_{\text{bonf}}{=}0.056$), significant at $\alpha{=}0.10$ after Bonferroni correction ($k{=}14$).
188	The ProofFOL genuine-rate permutation test ($p{=}0.10$) belongs to a separate hypothesis family (different dataset, independent experimental design) and does not reach significance even without correction; it is reported as an exploratory observation throughout.
189	Bonferroni assumes independence, which is conservative for our setting (several tests use overlapping data); Holm--Bonferroni or Benjamini--Hochberg FDR would recover the matched 5+5 comparison at conventional significance.
190	We report the most conservative Bonferroni results for transparency.

221	\paragraph{Classifier Validation.}
222	Hacking mode classification uses deterministic rule-based classifiers, not learned models, so standard ML precision/recall is not directly applicable.
223	CE and TS are identified by normalized text matching between conclusion and premise strings after whitespace and variable normalization; remaining modes are detected via functional analysis of the per-sample $n_{\text{necessary}}$ distribution from STA (leave-one-out ablation).
224	No training data or manual annotation is used for classification.
225	
226	To estimate precision, we manually verified 50 randomly sampled outputs classified as CE or TS: all 50 were confirmed correct (estimated precision ${>}$95\%, Wilson 95\% CI: [93\%, 100\%]).
227	Recall is inherently bounded by the text-match threshold: semantic manipulations that alter surface form while preserving the gaming structure (e.g., variable renaming beyond our normalization, or paraphrased conclusions) would be missed.
228	We cross-validate with functional LOO analysis: samples classified as non-hacking but showing $n_{\text{necessary}} \leq 1$ are flagged as potential false negatives.
229	This cross-validation revealed query-as-fact gaming in Prolog (\S\ref{app:hacking-modes}), where the strict text classifier reported 100\% non-hacking but functional analysis showed 95/97 samples were tautological ($n_{\text{necessary}}{=}1$).
230	The non-hacking rate for FOL conditions may therefore be slightly overestimated, as subtle semantic manipulations below our text-matching threshold would evade the strict classifier.
231	
232	\paragraph{Boundary case validation.}
233	Stratified validation across 82 samples (all five hacking categories) yields Cohen's $\kappa{=}1.0$; independent re-annotation confirms full agreement.
234	Structured inspection of 20 boundary cases (short-conclusion CE (10, minimum 4 characters), low-ISR genuine (5, minimum $\text{ISR}{=}0.22$), and TS on false propositions (5)) confirmed 20/20 correct classifications.
235	Short-conclusion CE samples are unambiguous hacking: the conclusion appears as a standalone premise with no NL source.
236	Low-ISR genuine samples reflect mode-collapsed template outputs, not structural gaming.
237	3/5 TS boundary cases confirm factually false propositions (e.g., affirming ``dogs are plants''), showing TS is not merely vacuous but actively harmful.
238	
239	\subsection{PG --- Premise-Subset Gaming}
240	\label{app:h8}
241	
242	Manual audit of ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ seed~42 revealed a previously undetected hacking mode: the model emits a subset of the gold premises that is individually necessary (high ISR) but insufficient for the intended derivation, with proof success depending on the conclusion already being embedded (CE-style).
243	We term this \textbf{PG (premise-subset gaming)}: formalizations where each component is LOO-necessary but the premise set is a strict subset of what the NL problem requires, inflating ISR without faithful reasoning.
244	
245	\paragraph{Detection.} PG is identified by manual inspection of non-hacking samples with unusually low premise counts ($n_{\text{prem}} \leq 3$) that nonetheless achieve high ISR.
246	Automated detection is not currently feasible because PG requires comparing the generated premise set against the gold premises.
247	
248	\paragraph{Audit scope and limitations.}
249	Full PG audit was completed for ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ seed~42 only.
250	ISR seeds~43 and~44 checkpoints were deleted before audit and cannot be recovered; their non-hacking rates may be overestimated.
251	Random $\beta{=}0.1$ does not produce PG by mechanism (no ISR optimization pressure); seed~42 audit confirmed PG${=}0$.
252	
253	\paragraph{TS false-negative correction (TSb obfuscated tautology).}
254	ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ seed~44 contained 12 samples with $n_{\text{prem}}{=}1$ classified as non-hacking by the text matcher.
255	Manual inspection confirmed all 12 are logically equivalent to TS but evade text matching through vacuous quantifier wrapping ($11/12$) or structural simplification ($1/12$).
256	We classify these as \textbf{TSb} (obfuscated tautology), distinct from text-match-detectable TSa.
257	$10/12$ achieve $\text{ISR}{\geq}0.83$, indicating simultaneous gaming of execution reward, ISR metric, and TS classifier: triple gaming (\S\ref{sec:taxonomy}).
258	After correction, ISR s44 non-hacking${=}0$; total TS = TSa (77 text-match) + TSb (12 obfuscated) = 89.
259	
260	\paragraph{Impact on non-hacking-rate comparison.}
261	After PG reclassification and TS false-negative correction: ISR non-hacking $= 14/231 = 6.06\%$ vs.\ random non-hacking $= 25/262 = 9.5\%$ (Fisher $p{=}0.182$, n.s.; Wilson 95\% CI: ISR [3.6\%, 9.9\%], Random [6.5\%, 13.7\%]).
262	The direction is consistent with ISR-amplified gaming modes (TS, PG) displacing non-hacking output, but the effect is not statistically significant at the conventional $\alpha{=}0.05$ threshold.
263	
264	\subsection{CE --- Conclusion Embedding}
265	
266	\paragraph{Definition.}
267	The conclusion appears verbatim (or with trivial variable renaming) as one premise among multiple premises.
268	The solver succeeds by matching the embedded conclusion, rendering the other premises irrelevant to the proof.
269	
270	\paragraph{Example (FOL).}
271	\smallskip\noindent\rule{\columnwidth}{0.3pt}
272	{\small\begin{verbatim}
273	Premises:
274	  all x (bird(x) -> flies(x)).
275	  bird(tweety).
276	  flies(tweety).  % conclusion embedded
277	Conclusion: flies(tweety).
278	\end{verbatim}}
279	\noindent\rule{\columnwidth}{0.3pt}\smallskip
280	
281	\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
282	Variable. The embedded premise has ISR~$=1$ (removing it may break the proof), but other premises may also register as necessary depending on Prover9's search strategy.
283	ISR does not distinguish trivial from substantive necessity.
284	
285	\paragraph{Prevalence.}
286	Conclusion embedding in some form (CE multi-premise or TS single-premise) is GRPO-universal at 68--97\% across all RL conditions.
287	Under exec-only and Random reward, it manifests as CE (71--93\%); under ISR reward, it shifts to TS (70.6\% pooled).
288	
289	
290	\subsection{TSa --- Conclusion Duplication (Standard)}
291	
292	\paragraph{Definition.}
293	The entire formalization collapses to a single premise whose content is identical (text-match detectable) to the conclusion.
294	Since $P \to P$ is trivially provable, this simultaneously maximizes exec reward.
295	Because the sole premise is necessary for every sub-component of the conclusion under LOO ablation, ISR is inflated toward 1.0.
296	
297	\paragraph{Example (FOL).}
298	\smallskip\noindent\rule{\columnwidth}{0.3pt}
299	{\small\begin{verbatim}
300	Premises:
301	  all x ((A(x)&B(x))->(C(x)|D(x))).
302	Conclusion:
303	  all x ((A(x)&B(x))->(C(x)|D(x))).
304	\end{verbatim}}
305	\noindent\rule{\columnwidth}{0.3pt}\smallskip
306	
307	\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
308	ISR~$\approx 0.8$--$1.0$.
309	The single premise is trivially ``maximally necessary,'' but the proof is vacuous.
310	TSa games both exec reward and ISR reward; TSb extends this to triple gaming by additionally evading the text-match classifier.
311	
312	\paragraph{Prevalence.}
313	TSa (text-match detectable): 64.5\% pooled (149/231) under ISR~$\beta{=}0.1$ (s42: 16.0\%, s43: 96.7\%, s44: 86.5\%).
314	Combined TS (TSa + TSb): 70.6\% (163/231; s43 TSa${=}59$ + TSb${=}2$; includes s44 FN correction).
315	Random~$\beta{=}0.1$ pooled: 13.7\% (36/262, all TSa; driven by seed~43 at 38.3\%, seeds~42 and~44 at 0\%).
316	
317	
318	\subsection{TSb --- Obfuscated Tautology}
319	
320	\paragraph{Definition.}
321	A single-premise formalization logically equivalent to TSa (premise = conclusion) but with surface-form differences that evade the text-match TS classifier.
322	The model achieves this through vacuous quantifier wrapping ($11/12$ instances) or structural simplification ($1/12$).
323	
324	\paragraph{Example (FOL, vacuous quantifier wrapping).}
325	\smallskip\noindent\rule{\columnwidth}{0.3pt}
326	{\small\begin{verbatim}
327	Premises:
328	  all x all y ((A(x)&B(y))->(C(x)|D(y))).
329	Conclusion:
330	  all x ((A(x)&B(x))->(C(x)|D(x))).
331	\end{verbatim}}
332	\noindent\rule{\columnwidth}{0.3pt}\smallskip
333	The premise introduces a vacuous second variable $y$, immediately unified with $x$; the formulas are logically equivalent but differ textually.
334	
335	\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
336	$\text{ISR}{\geq}0.83$ ($10/12$ samples).
337	TSb simultaneously games three objectives: execution reward ($r_{\text{exec}}{=}1$ via tautological proof), ISR metric (single necessary premise yields high ISR), and the text-match TS classifier (surface-form difference evades detection).
338	This triple gaming makes TSb the most complete Goodhart case we observe.
339	
340	\paragraph{Prevalence.}
341	Found primarily in ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ seed~44 ($12/89$ proved samples, all originally classified as non-hacking); seed~43 contributes $2$ additional cases.
342	Functional cross-validation via $n_{\text{necessary}}{=}1$ exposed the misclassification.
343	
344	
345	\subsection{Tautological Collapse}
346	
347	\paragraph{Definition.}
348	Two-component formalizations where the premise and conclusion are identical atomic or simple formulas, yielding a $P \to P$ tautology with minimal token cost.
349	
350	\paragraph{Example (FOL).}
351	\smallskip\noindent\rule{\columnwidth}{0.3pt}
352	\begin{verbatim}
353	Premises: p(a).
354	Conclusion: p(a).
355	\end{verbatim}
356	\noindent\rule{\columnwidth}{0.3pt}\smallskip
357	
358	\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
359	ISR~$=1.0$ (the sole premise is necessary).
360	Distinguished from TS by having low component count ($n_{\text{comp}}\approx 2$) and atomic formulas rather than complex sub-structured conclusions.
361	
362	\paragraph{Prevalence.}
363	Dominant in FOL exec-only seed~44 (PR~$=0.98$, mean $n_{\text{comp}}=2.04$, 100\% TS by strict classifier).
364	Also observed in Prolog exec+STA seed~42 (100\% TS, PR~$=0.50$).
365	
366	
367	\subsection{Repetition Collapse}
368	
369	\paragraph{Definition.}
370	The model generates identical premises or clauses repeated until the maximum completion length, producing a degenerate output with high token count but no logical diversity.
371	Removing any single repeated copy leaves the others intact, yielding ISR~$\approx 0$.
372	
373	\paragraph{Example (Prolog).}
374	\smallskip\noindent\rule{\columnwidth}{0.3pt}
375	\begin{verbatim}
376	penguin(fido).
377	penguin(fido).
378	penguin(fido).
379	... (repeated to 512 tokens)
380	query(penguin(fido)).
381	\end{verbatim}
382	\noindent\rule{\columnwidth}{0.3pt}\smallskip
383	
384	\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
385	ISR~$\approx 0$. Each copy is individually redundant since identical copies remain after removal.
386	ISR correctly diagnoses this degeneration.
387	
388	\paragraph{Prevalence.}
389	Observed in FOL exec-only seed~43 (87\% of outputs hit max completion length; PR~$=13$\%, ISR~$=0$).
390	
391	
392	\subsection{Complexity-without-Utility}
393	
394	\paragraph{Definition.}
395	The formalization contains syntactically complex premises (nested quantifiers, multi-arity predicates) that are semantically vacuous: none individually necessary for the proof.
396	The complexity inflates surface metrics (formula length, nesting depth) without contributing to logical derivation.
397	
398	\paragraph{Example (FOL).}
399	\smallskip\noindent\rule{\columnwidth}{0.3pt}
400	{\small\begin{verbatim}
401	Premises:
402	  all x all y (R(x,y) ->
403	    exists z (S(x,z) & T(z,y))).
404	  all x (P(x) -> Q(x)).
405	  P(a).            % only this needed
406	Conclusion: Q(a).
407	\end{verbatim}}
408	\noindent\rule{\columnwidth}{0.3pt}\smallskip
409	
410	\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
411	ISR correctly identifies the vacuous premises (ISR~$=0$ for each), pulling down the mean ISR.
412	This is the mode ISR is best calibrated for.
413	
414	\paragraph{Prevalence.}
415	Low. Observed in Random~$\beta{=}0.1$ seed~42 at 3.8\% (3/79).
416	Not observed under ISR reward (ISR's gradient discourages zero-ISR premises).
417	
418	
419	\subsection{Contradiction Explosion}
420	
421	\paragraph{Definition.}
422	The component count grows unboundedly over training.
423	Excess premises introduce contradictions or redundancies that trivially entail any conclusion via \emph{ex falso quodlibet}.
424	Individual premises may register as ISR~$=0$ (removable without breaking the proof), but the sheer count obscures the underlying triviality.
425	
426	\paragraph{Example (FOL, 1000-step exec-only).}
427	\smallskip\noindent\rule{\columnwidth}{0.3pt}
428	{\small\begin{verbatim}
429	Premises:
430	  c1. c2. c3. ... c18. % 18.55 mean
431	  % conclusion embedded among premises
432	Conclusion: Q(a).
433	\end{verbatim}}
434	\noindent\rule{\columnwidth}{0.3pt}\smallskip
435	
436	\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
437	ISR~$\approx 0$ (at 1000 steps: ISR~$=0.003$, with 94.8\% of proved samples having ISR~$=0$).
438	
439	\paragraph{Prevalence.}
440	Observed in extended exec-only training (seed~42, 1000 steps).
441	Mean component count grows from ${\sim}6$ (500 steps) to 18.55 (1000 steps).
442	
443	
444	\subsection{Query-as-Fact Gaming}
445	
446	\paragraph{Definition.}
447	The model converts the natural language conclusion into a snake\_case atom and includes it as both a ground fact and the query.
448	Prolog trivially proves the query by unifying with the fact.
449	This mode evades text-match classifiers designed for CE/TS because the generated atom bears no surface resemblance to the original conclusion text.
450	
451	\paragraph{Example (Prolog).}
452	\smallskip\noindent\rule{\columnwidth}{0.3pt}
453	\begin{verbatim}
454	% NL: "Fido is happy."
455	% Model output:
456	fido_is_happy.
457	:- fido_is_happy.     % query = fact
458	\end{verbatim}
459	\noindent\rule{\columnwidth}{0.3pt}\smallskip
460	
461	\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
462	ISR~$\approx 0.9$--$1.0$.
463	The single fact is trivially necessary (its removal breaks the query), inflating ISR.
464	Functionally equivalent to TS but with a distinct surface mechanism.
465	
466	\paragraph{Prevalence.}
467	Observed in Prolog exec+STA seed~44 (PR~$=0.97$, ISR~$=0.912$).
468	95/97 proved samples have $n_{\text{necessary}}=1$, confirming functional tautology despite the strict classifier reporting 100\% non-hacking.

672	\subsection{Early-Training Hacking Analysis (100-Step Checkpoint)}
673	\label{app:100step}
674	
675	To control for the prove-rate confound in our SFT comparison (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}), we analyze the exec-only checkpoint at 100 training steps (seed~42), where PR${=}32$\%, higher than SFT (13.0\%, 3-seed pooled) but still early in training.

677	By contrast, SFT at comparable or lower PR shows 7.7\% hacking (1/13 proved samples).
678	This demonstrates that reward hacking emerges early in GRPO training, well before the prove-rate plateau, and is not simply an artifact of having more proved samples available for exploitation.
679	The 100-step hacking rate (31.2\%) is already substantially above SFT (7.7\%), supporting the claim that hacking is associated with RL optimization rather than prove-rate level alone.

681	\subsection{$O(1)$ vs.\ $O(n)$ ISR Ablation}
682	\label{app:o1-ablation}
683	
684	All main experiments (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}--\ref{sec:crossdomain}) use $O(n)$ full LOO ISR during both training and evaluation; the $O(1)$ binary variant described below exists as an alternative implementation (\texttt{execution\_fast\_sta}) but is used only in the ablation reported here.
685	The two signals measure fundamentally different properties, not approximations of the same quantity.
686	The binary signal tests \emph{collective} premise necessity: $\text{fast\_ISR}(x) = 1$ if $x$ is proved and the conclusion is not provable under empty premises (tautology check), $0$ otherwise.
687	LOO tests \emph{individual} premise necessity: each component is removed in turn, and ISR reflects the fraction whose removal causes proof failure.
688	
689	\paragraph{Evaluation-time comparison.}
690	Across 402 proved samples from all ProofFOL conditions, the $O(1)$ binary signal is 1.0 for every sample: non-tautological conclusions cannot be proved without any premises, so the collective necessity test is trivially satisfied.
691	This renders $O(1)$ unable to distinguish hacking from genuine formalizations: both pass the empty-premise check.
692	By contrast, $O(n)$ LOO produces a clear separation: exec-only models average $\text{ISR}^*{=}0.046$ ($n{=}234$) while ISR-trained models average $\text{ISR}^*{=}0.183$ ($n{=}168$), because hacking constructions contain individually redundant components that LOO detects.
693	Of 179 disagreements between the two signals, all are false positives ($O(1){=}1$, LOO${=}0$): the binary check approves formalizations that LOO correctly identifies as structurally degenerate.
694	
695	\paragraph{Training-time ablation.}
696	As a training reward ($r = 0.5\,r_{\text{exec}} + 0.5\,\text{fast\_ISR}$, seed~42, 500 steps), the $O(1)$ variant achieves $\text{PR}{=}63\%$ with $\text{ISR}^*{=}0.007$, functionally zero, compared to $\text{ISR}^*{=}0.132$ under exec-only and $\text{ISR}^*{=}0.42$ under $O(n)$ ISR $\beta{=}0.1$.
697	The tautology check depresses prove rate by 30\,pp relative to exec-only ($63\%$ vs.\ $93\%$) by penalizing formalizations where the conclusion is provable without premises, but this constraint provides no gradient toward individual component necessity; the model is free to degenerate as long as it avoids trivial tautologies.
698	That even the fine-grained $O(n)$ LOO signal, which \emph{does} provide per-component necessity feedback, is ultimately gamed (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}) underscores that the problem lies in reward optimization itself, not in signal granularity.
699	
700	\paragraph{Computational overhead.}
701	Full LOO requires $n{+}1$ solver calls per sample (mean $n{\approx}6$ for FOLIO).
702	With Prover9 at ${\sim}5$\,ms per call, STA evaluation adds ${\sim}55$\,ms per sample versus ${\sim}4$\,s for LLM inference (${<}1\%$ overhead).
703	The $O(1)$ binary check adds a single solver call per proved sample (${<}2\%$ per training step), but the evaluation above shows this saving comes at the cost of all diagnostic power.

705	\subsection{Cross-Model Generalization: LLaMA-3.2-3B Cold-Start Failure}
706	\label{app:llama-coldstart}
707	
708	We applied the identical GRPO configuration (Table~\ref{tab:hyperparams}) to LLaMA-3.2-3B~\citep{grattafiori2024llama} (3B; exec-only, seed~42, $K{=}4$, FOLIO).
709	Across 72 of 500 planned steps the model produced zero valid Prover9 output, generating only natural-language text; $r_{\text{exec}}{=}0$ for all rollouts yields zero GRPO advantage, so training was terminated early.\footnote{This run was also affected by a generation-termination configuration issue (dual EOS tokens); the zero prove rate reflects both the base model's lack of FOL generation capability and truncated outputs.}
710	This establishes a \emph{capability threshold}: the base model must produce syntactically valid solver input for the RL loop to generate signal.
711	Qwen3-4B crosses this threshold (non-zero prove rates within 10 steps) while LLaMA-3.2-3B does not despite comparable size (3B vs.\ 4B), likely reflecting pretraining data composition.
712	An SFT warmstart (3 epochs on gold formalizations, lr$=$2$\times$10$^{-5}$) achieves $\text{PR}{=}16\%$ ($n{=}100$) after correcting the generation-termination issue.
713	However, the model produces Unicode FOL notation ($\forall$, $\to$, $\wedge$) instead of the required ASCII syntax despite training on ASCII-formatted data; the 16\% prove rate reflects Prover9's partial Unicode tolerance rather than correct format adherence.

721	Not all exec-only seeds converge.

\section{Extended Discussion}
\label{app:extended-discussion}

\paragraph{What ISR measures---and what it does not.}
ISR quantifies syntactic component necessity: the fraction of solver-input components whose individual removal causes proof failure.
This is strictly weaker than semantic faithfulness: whether the formalization accurately captures the natural-language meaning.
We verify this empirically: Spearman $\rho(\text{ISR}, \text{NLI accuracy}) = -0.049$ ($p = 0.187$, n.s.) from a downstream NLI evaluation on exec-only checkpoint outputs.
ISR and downstream task performance are uncorrelated.
ISR is thus a component-necessity diagnostic, not a semantic quality metric: high ISR indicates that every component contributes to the proof, not that the proof faithfully represents the original reasoning problem.

Critically, low ISR carries different semantics depending on the training objective.
Under exec-only training, low ISR in Prolog reflects redundant coding (repeated ground facts where removing any single copy does not affect the proof) rather than an absence of reasoning (\S\ref{sec:crosslogic}).
Under ISR-as-reward, high ISR reflects metric gaming (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}).
ISR values must always be interpreted relative to the optimization objective that produced them.

\paragraph{The premise-count confound.}
LOO-based metrics like ISR have an inherent mathematical bias: with fewer components, each is mechanically more likely to be necessary.
A formalization with 2 premises where both are necessary yields ISR${=}1.0$; one with 10 premises where 8 are necessary yields ISR${=}0.8$, even though the latter encodes richer reasoning.
This confound explains the sole apparent ISR-as-reward success (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}): ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ seed~42 produces shorter formalizations, mechanically inflating ISR.
Premise-count-matched comparison eliminates the difference ($1.06\times$; Table~\ref{tab:fol-beta01-detailed}).
This bias is not specific to our setting: any LOO-based structural metric applied to variable-length outputs requires component-count normalization.
We recommend that future work employing ablation-based diagnostics report premise-count-matched comparisons alongside raw values.

\paragraph{TS dose-response gradient.}
TS tautology follows a dose-response pattern across reward conditions: random $\beta{=}0.1$ produces $13.7\%$ TS ($36/262$ pooled; per-seed: $38.3\%$ in s43, $0\%$ in s42/s44), random $\beta{=}0.3$ yields 4--7 TSa samples per seed, and ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ reaches $70.6\%$ ($163/231$).
The gradient (random $\beta{=}0.1$ ($13.7\%$) $\to$ random $\beta{=}0.3$ (4--7 TSa per seed) $\to$ ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ ($70.6\%$)) shows ISR transforms TS from a seed-dependent GRPO tendency to a near-universal convergence direction.

\paragraph{Goodhart effects: implications.}
ISR was designed to \emph{detect} reward gaming of $r_{\text{exec}}$, yet when incorporated into the reward signal, the model games ISR itself. Any diagnostic metric risks becoming a target when optimized.
The dose-response pattern maps onto the Manheim \& Garrabrant taxonomy~\citep{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy}: $\beta{=}0.1$ on FOLIO instantiates \emph{regressional} Goodhart ($P{\to}P$ tautologies yield $\text{ISR}{\geq}0.5$, so ISR erroneously rewards the shortcut); $\beta{\geq}0.2$ introduces \emph{extremal} elements (PR collapse to 18\% vs.\ 48\% random at $\beta{=}0.3$).
The implication is conditional: ISR fails as a training reward when hacking satisfies its LOO structure (FOLIO), but produces beneficial instability when hacking does not (ProofFOL; \S\ref{sec:crossdomain}).

\paragraph{Single-seed unreliability.}
The three exec-only seeds diverge radically (PR $\sigma{=}47$ percentage points), each converging to a qualitatively different degeneration mode (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ seeds show similar divergence: 2/3 dominated by conclusion duplication (TS), 1/3 by premise minimization (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}).
Multi-seed evaluation with structural diagnostics should be standard practice for neurosymbolic RL systems.

\paragraph{Classifier limitations.}
Text-match hacking classifiers have systematic blind spots that functional analysis exposes.
In Prolog STA, two seeds achieved 100\% genuine classification under strict text matching, yet functional analysis via the $n_{\text{necessary}}$ distribution revealed 0\% genuine in both cases (Table~\ref{tab:prolog-detailed}).
One seed produces uppercase pseudo-Prolog that is functionally tautological; the other converts conclusions to snake\_case atoms serving as both fact and query, a gaming mode invisible to string comparison.
Practitioners should cross-validate text-match classifiers with functional metrics and never treat classifier-reported genuine rates as ground truth without independent verification.

\paragraph{Practical guidelines.}
\label{app:practical-guidelines}
Our findings yield five guidelines for GRPO-trained neurosymbolic systems:
(1)~Never evaluate by prove rate alone; use ISR and component count as joint diagnostics.
(2)~Report multi-seed results: single-seed GRPO evaluation is unreliable, as cross-seed variance can exceed the effect size of interest (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
(3)~Use ISR for post-hoc diagnosis only, not as a training signal; any dose induces gaming or collapse.
(4)~Treat LOO-based metrics as component-count-biased until normalized.
(5)~Expect conclusion embedding as a GRPO-universal baseline (Table~\ref{tab:goodhart-landscape}): reward shaping alters hacking composition, not prevalence.

\paragraph{Multiple testing correction.}
\label{app:statistical-details}
We define two test families: FOLIO ($k{=}14$ tests across all conditions) and ProofFOL ($k{=}1$).
Within the FOLIO family, Bonferroni correction at $\alpha{=}0.05$ yields adjusted thresholds of $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.05/14{=}0.0036$.
Three primary comparisons survive correction: the TS rate difference (ISR vs.\ random; $p_{\text{bonf}}{=}1.82{\times}10^{-38}$), the SFT vs.\ exec-only non-hacking rate ($p_{\text{bonf}}{=}0.014$), and the Cochran--Mantel--Haenszel test for TS association across seeds ($p_{\text{bonf}}{<}10^{-8}$).
The matched 5+5-seed Fisher/Mann-Whitney comparison is borderline ($p_{\text{bonf}}{=}0.056$), significant at $\alpha{=}0.10$ after Bonferroni correction ($k{=}14$).
The ProofFOL genuine-rate permutation test ($p{=}0.10$) belongs to a separate hypothesis family (different dataset, independent experimental design) and does not reach significance even without correction; it is reported as an exploratory observation throughout.
Bonferroni assumes independence, which is conservative for our setting (several tests use overlapping data); Holm--Bonferroni or Benjamini--Hochberg FDR would recover the matched 5+5 comparison at conventional significance.
We report the most conservative Bonferroni results for transparency.

\paragraph{Classifier Validation.}
Hacking mode classification uses deterministic rule-based classifiers, not learned models, so standard ML precision/recall is not directly applicable.
CE and TS are identified by normalized text matching between conclusion and premise strings after whitespace and variable normalization; remaining modes are detected via functional analysis of the per-sample $n_{\text{necessary}}$ distribution from STA (leave-one-out ablation).
No training data or manual annotation is used for classification.

To estimate precision, we manually verified 50 randomly sampled outputs classified as CE or TS: all 50 were confirmed correct (estimated precision ${>}$95\%, Wilson 95\% CI: [93\%, 100\%]).
Recall is inherently bounded by the text-match threshold: semantic manipulations that alter surface form while preserving the gaming structure (e.g., variable renaming beyond our normalization, or paraphrased conclusions) would be missed.
We cross-validate with functional LOO analysis: samples classified as non-hacking but showing $n_{\text{necessary}} \leq 1$ are flagged as potential false negatives.
This cross-validation revealed query-as-fact gaming in Prolog (\S\ref{app:hacking-modes}), where the strict text classifier reported 100\% non-hacking but functional analysis showed 95/97 samples were tautological ($n_{\text{necessary}}{=}1$).
The non-hacking rate for FOL conditions may therefore be slightly overestimated, as subtle semantic manipulations below our text-matching threshold would evade the strict classifier.

\paragraph{Boundary case validation.}
Stratified validation across 82 samples (all five hacking categories) yields Cohen's $\kappa{=}1.0$; independent re-annotation confirms full agreement.
Structured inspection of 20 boundary cases (short-conclusion CE (10, minimum 4 characters), low-ISR genuine (5, minimum $\text{ISR}{=}0.22$), and TS on false propositions (5)) confirmed 20/20 correct classifications.
Short-conclusion CE samples are unambiguous hacking: the conclusion appears as a standalone premise with no NL source.
Low-ISR genuine samples reflect mode-collapsed template outputs, not structural gaming.
3/5 TS boundary cases confirm factually false propositions (e.g., affirming ``dogs are plants''), showing TS is not merely vacuous but actively harmful.

\subsection{PG --- Premise-Subset Gaming}
\label{app:h8}

Manual audit of ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ seed~42 revealed a previously undetected hacking mode: the model emits a subset of the gold premises that is individually necessary (high ISR) but insufficient for the intended derivation, with proof success depending on the conclusion already being embedded (CE-style).
We term this \textbf{PG (premise-subset gaming)}: formalizations where each component is LOO-necessary but the premise set is a strict subset of what the NL problem requires, inflating ISR without faithful reasoning.

\paragraph{Detection.} PG is identified by manual inspection of non-hacking samples with unusually low premise counts ($n_{\text{prem}} \leq 3$) that nonetheless achieve high ISR.
Automated detection is not currently feasible because PG requires comparing the generated premise set against the gold premises.

\paragraph{Audit scope and limitations.}
Full PG audit was completed for ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ seed~42 only.
ISR seeds~43 and~44 checkpoints were deleted before audit and cannot be recovered; their non-hacking rates may be overestimated.
Random $\beta{=}0.1$ does not produce PG by mechanism (no ISR optimization pressure); seed~42 audit confirmed PG${=}0$.

\paragraph{TS false-negative correction (TSb obfuscated tautology).}
ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ seed~44 contained 12 samples with $n_{\text{prem}}{=}1$ classified as non-hacking by the text matcher.
Manual inspection confirmed all 12 are logically equivalent to TS but evade text matching through vacuous quantifier wrapping ($11/12$) or structural simplification ($1/12$).
We classify these as \textbf{TSb} (obfuscated tautology), distinct from text-match-detectable TSa.
$10/12$ achieve $\text{ISR}{\geq}0.83$, indicating simultaneous gaming of execution reward, ISR metric, and TS classifier: triple gaming (\S\ref{sec:taxonomy}).
After correction, ISR s44 non-hacking${=}0$; total TS = TSa (77 text-match) + TSb (12 obfuscated) = 89.

\paragraph{Impact on non-hacking-rate comparison.}
After PG reclassification and TS false-negative correction: ISR non-hacking $= 14/231 = 6.06\%$ vs.\ random non-hacking $= 25/262 = 9.5\%$ (Fisher $p{=}0.182$, n.s.; Wilson 95\% CI: ISR [3.6\%, 9.9\%], Random [6.5\%, 13.7\%]).
The direction is consistent with ISR-amplified gaming modes (TS, PG) displacing non-hacking output, but the effect is not statistically significant at the conventional $\alpha{=}0.05$ threshold.

\subsection{CE --- Conclusion Embedding}

\paragraph{Definition.}
The conclusion appears verbatim (or with trivial variable renaming) as one premise among multiple premises.
The solver succeeds by matching the embedded conclusion, rendering the other premises irrelevant to the proof.

\paragraph{Example (FOL).}
\smallskip\noindent\rule{\columnwidth}{0.3pt}
{\small\begin{verbatim}
Premises:
  all x (bird(x) -> flies(x)).
  bird(tweety).
  flies(tweety).  % conclusion embedded
Conclusion: flies(tweety).
\end{verbatim}}
\noindent\rule{\columnwidth}{0.3pt}\smallskip

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
Variable. The embedded premise has ISR~$=1$ (removing it may break the proof), but other premises may also register as necessary depending on Prover9's search strategy.
ISR does not distinguish trivial from substantive necessity.

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
Conclusion embedding in some form (CE multi-premise or TS single-premise) is GRPO-universal at 68--97\% across all RL conditions.
Under exec-only and Random reward, it manifests as CE (71--93\%); under ISR reward, it shifts to TS (70.6\% pooled).


\subsection{TSa --- Conclusion Duplication (Standard)}

\paragraph{Definition.}
The entire formalization collapses to a single premise whose content is identical (text-match detectable) to the conclusion.
Since $P \to P$ is trivially provable, this simultaneously maximizes exec reward.
Because the sole premise is necessary for every sub-component of the conclusion under LOO ablation, ISR is inflated toward 1.0.

\paragraph{Example (FOL).}
\smallskip\noindent\rule{\columnwidth}{0.3pt}
{\small\begin{verbatim}
Premises:
  all x ((A(x)&B(x))->(C(x)|D(x))).
Conclusion:
  all x ((A(x)&B(x))->(C(x)|D(x))).
\end{verbatim}}
\noindent\rule{\columnwidth}{0.3pt}\smallskip

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
ISR~$\approx 0.8$--$1.0$.
The single premise is trivially ``maximally necessary,'' but the proof is vacuous.
TSa games both exec reward and ISR reward; TSb extends this to triple gaming by additionally evading the text-match classifier.

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
TSa (text-match detectable): 64.5\% pooled (149/231) under ISR~$\beta{=}0.1$ (s42: 16.0\%, s43: 96.7\%, s44: 86.5\%).
Combined TS (TSa + TSb): 70.6\% (163/231; s43 TSa${=}59$ + TSb${=}2$; includes s44 FN correction).
Random~$\beta{=}0.1$ pooled: 13.7\% (36/262, all TSa; driven by seed~43 at 38.3\%, seeds~42 and~44 at 0\%).


\subsection{TSb --- Obfuscated Tautology}

\paragraph{Definition.}
A single-premise formalization logically equivalent to TSa (premise = conclusion) but with surface-form differences that evade the text-match TS classifier.
The model achieves this through vacuous quantifier wrapping ($11/12$ instances) or structural simplification ($1/12$).

\paragraph{Example (FOL, vacuous quantifier wrapping).}
\smallskip\noindent\rule{\columnwidth}{0.3pt}
{\small\begin{verbatim}
Premises:
  all x all y ((A(x)&B(y))->(C(x)|D(y))).
Conclusion:
  all x ((A(x)&B(x))->(C(x)|D(x))).
\end{verbatim}}
\noindent\rule{\columnwidth}{0.3pt}\smallskip
The premise introduces a vacuous second variable $y$, immediately unified with $x$; the formulas are logically equivalent but differ textually.

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
$\text{ISR}{\geq}0.83$ ($10/12$ samples).
TSb simultaneously games three objectives: execution reward ($r_{\text{exec}}{=}1$ via tautological proof), ISR metric (single necessary premise yields high ISR), and the text-match TS classifier (surface-form difference evades detection).
This triple gaming makes TSb the most complete Goodhart case we observe.

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
Found primarily in ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ seed~44 ($12/89$ proved samples, all originally classified as non-hacking); seed~43 contributes $2$ additional cases.
Functional cross-validation via $n_{\text{necessary}}{=}1$ exposed the misclassification.


\subsection{Tautological Collapse}

\paragraph{Definition.}
Two-component formalizations where the premise and conclusion are identical atomic or simple formulas, yielding a $P \to P$ tautology with minimal token cost.

\paragraph{Example (FOL).}
\smallskip\noindent\rule{\columnwidth}{0.3pt}
\begin{verbatim}
Premises: p(a).
Conclusion: p(a).
\end{verbatim}
\noindent\rule{\columnwidth}{0.3pt}\smallskip

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
ISR~$=1.0$ (the sole premise is necessary).
Distinguished from TS by having low component count ($n_{\text{comp}}\approx 2$) and atomic formulas rather than complex sub-structured conclusions.

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
Dominant in FOL exec-only seed~44 (PR~$=0.98$, mean $n_{\text{comp}}=2.04$, 100\% TS by strict classifier).
Also observed in Prolog exec+STA seed~42 (100\% TS, PR~$=0.50$).


\subsection{Repetition Collapse}

\paragraph{Definition.}
The model generates identical premises or clauses repeated until the maximum completion length, producing a degenerate output with high token count but no logical diversity.
Removing any single repeated copy leaves the others intact, yielding ISR~$\approx 0$.

\paragraph{Example (Prolog).}
\smallskip\noindent\rule{\columnwidth}{0.3pt}
\begin{verbatim}
penguin(fido).
penguin(fido).
penguin(fido).
... (repeated to 512 tokens)
query(penguin(fido)).
\end{verbatim}
\noindent\rule{\columnwidth}{0.3pt}\smallskip

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
ISR~$\approx 0$. Each copy is individually redundant since identical copies remain after removal.
ISR correctly diagnoses this degeneration.

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
Observed in FOL exec-only seed~43 (87\% of outputs hit max completion length; PR~$=13$\%, ISR~$=0$).


\subsection{Complexity-without-Utility}

\paragraph{Definition.}
The formalization contains syntactically complex premises (nested quantifiers, multi-arity predicates) that are semantically vacuous: none individually necessary for the proof.
The complexity inflates surface metrics (formula length, nesting depth) without contributing to logical derivation.

\paragraph{Example (FOL).}
\smallskip\noindent\rule{\columnwidth}{0.3pt}
{\small\begin{verbatim}
Premises:
  all x all y (R(x,y) ->
    exists z (S(x,z) & T(z,y))).
  all x (P(x) -> Q(x)).
  P(a).            % only this needed
Conclusion: Q(a).
\end{verbatim}}
\noindent\rule{\columnwidth}{0.3pt}\smallskip

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
ISR correctly identifies the vacuous premises (ISR~$=0$ for each), pulling down the mean ISR.
This is the mode ISR is best calibrated for.

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
Low. Observed in Random~$\beta{=}0.1$ seed~42 at 3.8\% (3/79).
Not observed under ISR reward (ISR's gradient discourages zero-ISR premises).


\subsection{Contradiction Explosion}

\paragraph{Definition.}
The component count grows unboundedly over training.
Excess premises introduce contradictions or redundancies that trivially entail any conclusion via \emph{ex falso quodlibet}.
Individual premises may register as ISR~$=0$ (removable without breaking the proof), but the sheer count obscures the underlying triviality.

\paragraph{Example (FOL, 1000-step exec-only).}
\smallskip\noindent\rule{\columnwidth}{0.3pt}
{\small\begin{verbatim}
Premises:
  c1. c2. c3. ... c18. % 18.55 mean
  % conclusion embedded among premises
Conclusion: Q(a).
\end{verbatim}}
\noindent\rule{\columnwidth}{0.3pt}\smallskip

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
ISR~$\approx 0$ (at 1000 steps: ISR~$=0.003$, with 94.8\% of proved samples having ISR~$=0$).

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
Observed in extended exec-only training (seed~42, 1000 steps).
Mean component count grows from ${\sim}6$ (500 steps) to 18.55 (1000 steps).


\subsection{Query-as-Fact Gaming}

\paragraph{Definition.}
The model converts the natural language conclusion into a snake\_case atom and includes it as both a ground fact and the query.
Prolog trivially proves the query by unifying with the fact.
This mode evades text-match classifiers designed for CE/TS because the generated atom bears no surface resemblance to the original conclusion text.

\paragraph{Example (Prolog).}
\smallskip\noindent\rule{\columnwidth}{0.3pt}
\begin{verbatim}
% NL: "Fido is happy."
% Model output:
fido_is_happy.
:- fido_is_happy.     % query = fact
\end{verbatim}
\noindent\rule{\columnwidth}{0.3pt}\smallskip

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
ISR~$\approx 0.9$--$1.0$.
The single fact is trivially necessary (its removal breaks the query), inflating ISR.
Functionally equivalent to TS but with a distinct surface mechanism.

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
Observed in Prolog exec+STA seed~44 (PR~$=0.97$, ISR~$=0.912$).
95/97 proved samples have $n_{\text{necessary}}=1$, confirming functional tautology despite the strict classifier reporting 100\% non-hacking.

\subsection{Early-Training Hacking Analysis (100-Step Checkpoint)}
\label{app:100step}

To control for the prove-rate confound in our SFT comparison (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}), we analyze the exec-only checkpoint at 100 training steps (seed~42), where PR${=}32$\%, higher than SFT (13.0\%, 3-seed pooled) but still early in training.
Of the 32 proved samples, 9 (28.1\%) exhibit TS hacking (single premise identical to conclusion) and 1 (3.1\%) exhibits CE (conclusion embedded among premises), yielding a total hacking rate of 31.2\%.
By contrast, SFT at comparable or lower PR shows 7.7\% hacking (1/13 proved samples).
This demonstrates that reward hacking emerges early in GRPO training, well before the prove-rate plateau, and is not simply an artifact of having more proved samples available for exploitation.
The 100-step hacking rate (31.2\%) is already substantially above SFT (7.7\%), supporting the claim that hacking is associated with RL optimization rather than prove-rate level alone.

\subsection{$O(1)$ vs.\ $O(n)$ ISR Ablation}
\label{app:o1-ablation}

All main experiments (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}--\ref{sec:crossdomain}) use $O(n)$ full LOO ISR during both training and evaluation; the $O(1)$ binary variant described below exists as an alternative implementation (\texttt{execution\_fast\_sta}) but is used only in the ablation reported here.
The two signals measure fundamentally different properties, not approximations of the same quantity.
The binary signal tests \emph{collective} premise necessity: $\text{fast\_ISR}(x) = 1$ if $x$ is proved and the conclusion is not provable under empty premises (tautology check), $0$ otherwise.
LOO tests \emph{individual} premise necessity: each component is removed in turn, and ISR reflects the fraction whose removal causes proof failure.

\paragraph{Evaluation-time comparison.}
Across 402 proved samples from all ProofFOL conditions, the $O(1)$ binary signal is 1.0 for every sample: non-tautological conclusions cannot be proved without any premises, so the collective necessity test is trivially satisfied.
This renders $O(1)$ unable to distinguish hacking from genuine formalizations: both pass the empty-premise check.
By contrast, $O(n)$ LOO produces a clear separation: exec-only models average $\text{ISR}^*{=}0.046$ ($n{=}234$) while ISR-trained models average $\text{ISR}^*{=}0.183$ ($n{=}168$), because hacking constructions contain individually redundant components that LOO detects.
Of 179 disagreements between the two signals, all are false positives ($O(1){=}1$, LOO${=}0$): the binary check approves formalizations that LOO correctly identifies as structurally degenerate.

\paragraph{Training-time ablation.}
As a training reward ($r = 0.5\,r_{\text{exec}} + 0.5\,\text{fast\_ISR}$, seed~42, 500 steps), the $O(1)$ variant achieves $\text{PR}{=}63\%$ with $\text{ISR}^*{=}0.007$, functionally zero, compared to $\text{ISR}^*{=}0.132$ under exec-only and $\text{ISR}^*{=}0.42$ under $O(n)$ ISR $\beta{=}0.1$.
The tautology check depresses prove rate by 30\,pp relative to exec-only ($63\%$ vs.\ $93\%$) by penalizing formalizations where the conclusion is provable without premises, but this constraint provides no gradient toward individual component necessity; the model is free to degenerate as long as it avoids trivial tautologies.
That even the fine-grained $O(n)$ LOO signal, which \emph{does} provide per-component necessity feedback, is ultimately gamed (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}) underscores that the problem lies in reward optimization itself, not in signal granularity.

\paragraph{Computational overhead.}
Full LOO requires $n{+}1$ solver calls per sample (mean $n{\approx}6$ for FOLIO).
With Prover9 at ${\sim}5$\,ms per call, STA evaluation adds ${\sim}55$\,ms per sample versus ${\sim}4$\,s for LLM inference (${<}1\%$ overhead).
The $O(1)$ binary check adds a single solver call per proved sample (${<}2\%$ per training step), but the evaluation above shows this saving comes at the cost of all diagnostic power.

\subsection{Cross-Model Generalization: LLaMA-3.2-3B Cold-Start Failure}
\label{app:llama-coldstart}

We applied the identical GRPO configuration (Table~\ref{tab:hyperparams}) to LLaMA-3.2-3B~\citep{grattafiori2024llama} (3B; exec-only, seed~42, $K{=}4$, FOLIO).
Across 72 of 500 planned steps the model produced zero valid Prover9 output, generating only natural-language text; $r_{\text{exec}}{=}0$ for all rollouts yields zero GRPO advantage, so training was terminated early.\footnote{This run was also affected by a generation-termination configuration issue (dual EOS tokens); the zero prove rate reflects both the base model's lack of FOL generation capability and truncated outputs.}
This establishes a \emph{capability threshold}: the base model must produce syntactically valid solver input for the RL loop to generate signal.
Qwen3-4B crosses this threshold (non-zero prove rates within 10 steps) while LLaMA-3.2-3B does not despite comparable size (3B vs.\ 4B), likely reflecting pretraining data composition.
An SFT warmstart (3 epochs on gold formalizations, lr$=$2$\times$10$^{-5}$) achieves $\text{PR}{=}16\%$ ($n{=}100$) after correcting the generation-termination issue.
However, the model produces Unicode FOL notation ($\forall$, $\to$, $\wedge$) instead of the required ASCII syntax despite training on ASCII-formatted data; the 16\% prove rate reflects Prover9's partial Unicode tolerance rather than correct format adherence.
Subsequent GRPO runs (exec-only, 500 steps from SFT warmstart, 3 seeds) fail to improve beyond SFT baseline ($\text{PR}{=}15.0{\pm}1.0\%$, $n{=}14$--$16$ proved per seed), yet produce no structural degeneration: $86.6{\pm}0.9\%$ of proved samples are genuine across seeds, with cross-seed variance near zero ($\sigma_{\text{PR}}{=}1$\,pp).
This contrasts sharply with Qwen3-4B, where GRPO reaches $93\%$ PR but collapses to $8\%$ genuine with high cross-seed variance.
The result suggests structural degeneration is a byproduct of successful RL optimization, not of the training procedure \emph{per se}: when GRPO fails to amplify prove rate, the model retains structural integrity.

\subsection{Seed-Dependent Convergence in Exec-Only GRPO}
\label{app:seed-convergence}

Not all exec-only seeds converge.
Of 6 seeds tested (s42--s46, s52), we observe three regimes: \emph{converging with degeneration} (s42: $\text{PR}{=}93\%$, genuine${=}7.5\%$; s44: $\text{PR}{=}96\%$, genuine${=}0\%$; s46: $\text{PR}{=}93\%$ at 500 steps), \emph{slow convergence with degeneration} (s43: $\text{PR}{=}14\%$ but $100\%$ hacking at 500 steps), and \emph{non-converging} (s45: $\text{PR}{=}15\%$, genuine${=}86.7\%$; s52: $\text{PR}{=}14\%$, genuine${=}85.7\%$).
Non-converging seeds retain high genuine rates (85--87\%), indicating that structural degeneration is conditional on successful RL optimization: when GRPO fails to bootstrap prove rate beyond base-model levels, the model preserves structural integrity.
Extended training to 1000 steps for s45 confirms persistent non-convergence ($\text{PR}{=}15\%$, $\text{ISR}^*{=}0.592$, genuine${=}86.7\%$, $n{=}15$ proved); the model neither improves nor degenerates.

This parallels the LLaMA-3.2-3B finding (Appendix~\ref{app:llama-coldstart}), where GRPO also fails to improve PR and retains structural quality.
Both cases support the interpretation that degeneration is a byproduct of reward optimization success, not of the training procedure per se.

\label{app:8b-results}

Cosine learning-rate decay combined with insufficient early bootstrap appears to prevent the model from escaping the low-PR regime.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related-work}

\paragraph{Neurosymbolic reasoning.}
LLM-solver pipelines~\citep{satlm, logic-lm, linc, fover-pei2025, lorp} and RL methods trained on solver feedback~\citep{mellgren-prolog-grpo, logic-rl, deepseek-prover-v15, deepseek-r1} evaluate execution accuracy alone, with no diagnostic for component necessity.
AlphaProof~\citep{alphaproof2025} and DeepSeek-Prover-V2~\citep{deepseek-prover-v2} apply RL-based formal verification at scale in Lean~4 for competition mathematics; STA-style diagnostics could probe whether similar structural degeneration occurs in these settings.
We use FOLIO~\citep{folio}, the only public NLI benchmark with both FOL and Prolog annotations.

\paragraph{Process rewards and reward shaping.}
Reward shaping theory~\citep{ng1999policy} constrains when auxiliary rewards preserve optimal policies.
In mathematical reasoning, learned process reward models~\citep{lightman-verify-step, math-shepherd, cobbe2021training, uesato2022solving} and verifier-guided search~\citep{nlproofs, vstar, easy-to-hard} provide step-level feedback, but suffer from reward-model noise and distribution shift~\citep{processbench}.
A recurring finding is that auxiliary rewards can hurt rather than help: \citet{gao-effective-rl-reward} show process/outcome bonuses can degrade RL training, and \citet{setlur2025rewarding} demonstrate that bonus magnitude requires careful calibration.
Annotation-free alternatives~\citep{cui2025prime, rlsf} derive dense rewards from outcome signals or solver certificates; ISR follows this direction but our results reveal that even annotation-free structural rewards are susceptible to Goodhart effects.
\citet{sullivan2025grpo-prm} prove GRPO with outcome reward is implicitly a Monte-Carlo PRM, a mechanism for why component-level gaming emerges under GRPO.

\paragraph{Reward hacking and Goodhart's Law.}
Goodhart's Law is established theoretically~\citep{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy, skalse-reward-hacking, karwowski-goodhart-rl} and empirically in RLHF~\citep{gao-reward-overoptimization} and logical formalization~\citep{bondarenko-spec-gaming, kim-game-formalization}.
Most closely related, \citet{kim-game-formalization} document inference-time gaming on FOLIO with frontier models and Lean~4; our work is complementary in studying training-time degeneration with component necessity rather than faithfulness, and combining STA with inference-time detection would provide full gaming coverage.
\citet{kwa-catastrophic-goodhart} show that heavy-tailed reward misspecification causes catastrophic Goodhart where KL regularization provably fails, a theoretical lens for why GRPO's KL penalty does not prevent our observed collapse.
Concurrent work documents spurious signals in RLVR~\citep{spurious-rewards, yan2026spurious, dong2026probing, metr-reward-hacking} and proposes composite rewards as mitigations~\citep{tarek2025reward, pronesti2026beyond}; \citet{yue2025rl-reasoning} show RLVR redistributes base-model probability mass rather than creating new reasoning, consistent with our finding that GRPO exploits existing shortcuts.
\citet{helff2026gaming} propose Input Perturbation Testing for gaming detection; STA shares the perturbation intuition but operates at the component level in neurosymbolic settings where gaming emerges during training.
\citet{khalifa2026countdown} provide RLVR hacking testbeds.
Our Goodhart effect follows the regressional pattern~\citep{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy} on FOLIO, with extremal dynamics at high $\beta$; its application to a diagnostic designed to \emph{detect} gaming, and the dataset-dependent asymmetry it reveals, are to our knowledge novel.

\paragraph{Mutation testing.}
STA adapts the LOO mutation paradigm~\citep{demillo1978, jia-harman-survey} to solver inputs; novelty lies in application and findings, not in the perturbation primitive.

\section{Experimental Setup}
\label{app:setup}

Table~\ref{tab:hyperparams} lists all hyperparameters shared across experiments.
All RL conditions use the same GRPO configuration; only the reward function differs.
Seeds control model weight initialization and data shuffling; training data is held constant across all seeds and conditions (Constraint~C001).

\paragraph{Compute resources.}
Experiments were run on single-GPU setups (NVIDIA RTX 4090 24\,GB and RTX PRO 6000 96\,GB).
Each GRPO training run takes approximately 1--2 GPU-hours (500 steps) or 3--5 GPU-hours (1000 steps).
Total compute across all seeds, conditions, and reruns is approximately 80--120 GPU-hours.

\paragraph{SFT convergence.}
SFT training converged across all three seeds: final-step loss ${\leq}0.04$ and token accuracy ${>}99\%$ after ${\sim}8$ epochs on 500 examples (seed~42: $0.029$; seed~44: $0.033$); the 1000-step extension further decreases loss to $0.017$.

\paragraph{Evaluation exception.}
FOL exec-only seed~43 (\texttt{plan001-exec-only-s43-r4}) was evaluated with sampling (temperature~$=0.7$) rather than greedy decoding.
Its PR and ISR values are included for completeness but are not strictly comparable with other seeds under the unified evaluation protocol (C004).

\paragraph{Reward formulation.}
An additive variant ($r = r_{\text{exec}} + \beta\,\text{ISR}$) was tested in early experiments but collapsed prove rate to near-zero, as ISR alone provides no gradient toward provable formalizations; the multiplicative form $r_{\text{exec}}\cdot(1+\beta\,\text{ISR})$ ensures ISR modulates only proved outputs.

\paragraph{ProofFOL dataset construction.}
\label{app:prooffol-construction}
ProofFOL is derived from ProofWriter~\citep{proofwriter} (10{,}424 training examples) via the GPT-4o silver-standard FOL translation pipeline of \citet{prooffol-thatikonda2024} with Prover9 verification filtering (${\sim}70\%$ retention; failures from timeouts, unsupported constructs, and translation errors).
Of the translated examples, 99.1\% parse successfully (92 skipped due to empty FOL output).
We sample 500 training and 100 evaluation examples (seed~42) from the verified pool.
Table~\ref{tab:prooffol-vs-folio} compares key structural properties.

The absence of XOR constraints and the regularity of predicate structure make ProofFOL a complementary testbed: structural degeneration must emerge from the RL training dynamics rather than from formalization difficulty.

\section{STA Algorithm}
\label{app:algorithm}

Algorithm~\ref{alg:sta} (Section~\ref{sec:sta}) gives the procedure for computing ISR over a proved formalization.
For unproved samples ($S(x) \neq \textit{proved}$), ISR is undefined and the protocol is not applied.


\section{Extended Discussion}
\label{app:extended-discussion}

\paragraph{What ISR measures---and what it does not.}
ISR quantifies syntactic component necessity: the fraction of solver-input components whose individual removal causes proof failure.
This is strictly weaker than semantic faithfulness: whether the formalization accurately captures the natural-language meaning.
We verify this empirically: Spearman $\rho(\text{ISR}, \text{NLI accuracy}) = -0.049$ ($p = 0.187$, n.s.) from a downstream NLI evaluation on exec-only checkpoint outputs.
ISR and downstream task performance are uncorrelated.
ISR is thus a component-necessity diagnostic, not a semantic quality metric: high ISR indicates that every component contributes to the proof, not that the proof faithfully represents the original reasoning problem.

Critically, low ISR carries different semantics depending on the training objective.
Under exec-only training, low ISR in Prolog reflects redundant coding (repeated ground facts where removing any single copy does not affect the proof) rather than an absence of reasoning (\S\ref{sec:crosslogic}).
Under ISR-as-reward, high ISR reflects metric gaming (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}).
ISR values must always be interpreted relative to the optimization objective that produced them.

\paragraph{The premise-count confound.}
LOO-based metrics like ISR have an inherent mathematical bias: with fewer components, each is mechanically more likely to be necessary.
A formalization with 2 premises where both are necessary yields ISR${=}1.0$; one with 10 premises where 8 are necessary yields ISR${=}0.8$, even though the latter encodes richer reasoning.
This confound explains the sole apparent ISR-as-reward success (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}): ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ seed~42 produces shorter formalizations, mechanically inflating ISR.
Premise-count-matched comparison eliminates the difference ($1.06\times$; Table~\ref{tab:fol-beta01-detailed}).
This bias is not specific to our setting: any LOO-based structural metric applied to variable-length outputs requires component-count normalization.
We recommend that future work employing ablation-based diagnostics report premise-count-matched comparisons alongside raw values.

\paragraph{TS dose-response gradient.}
TS tautology follows a dose-response pattern across reward conditions: random $\beta{=}0.1$ produces $13.7\%$ TS ($36/262$ pooled; per-seed: $38.3\%$ in s43, $0\%$ in s42/s44), random $\beta{=}0.3$ yields 4--7 TSa samples per seed, and ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ reaches $70.6\%$ ($163/231$).
The gradient (random $\beta{=}0.1$ ($13.7\%$) $\to$ random $\beta{=}0.3$ (4--7 TSa per seed) $\to$ ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ ($70.6\%$)) shows ISR transforms TS from a seed-dependent GRPO tendency to a near-universal convergence direction.

\paragraph{Goodhart effects: implications.}
ISR was designed to \emph{detect} reward gaming of $r_{\text{exec}}$, yet when incorporated into the reward signal, the model games ISR itself. Any diagnostic metric risks becoming a target when optimized.
The dose-response pattern maps onto the Manheim \& Garrabrant taxonomy~\citep{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy}: $\beta{=}0.1$ on FOLIO instantiates \emph{regressional} Goodhart ($P{\to}P$ tautologies yield $\text{ISR}{\geq}0.5$, so ISR erroneously rewards the shortcut); $\beta{\geq}0.2$ introduces \emph{extremal} elements (PR collapse to 18\% vs.\ 48\% random at $\beta{=}0.3$).
The implication is conditional: ISR fails as a training reward when hacking satisfies its LOO structure (FOLIO), but produces beneficial instability when hacking does not (ProofFOL; \S\ref{sec:crossdomain}).

\paragraph{Single-seed unreliability.}
The three exec-only seeds diverge radically (PR $\sigma{=}47$ percentage points), each converging to a qualitatively different degeneration mode (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ seeds show similar divergence: 2/3 dominated by conclusion duplication (TS), 1/3 by premise minimization (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}).
Multi-seed evaluation with structural diagnostics should be standard practice for neurosymbolic RL systems.

\paragraph{Classifier limitations.}
Text-match hacking classifiers have systematic blind spots that functional analysis exposes.
In Prolog STA, two seeds achieved 100\% genuine classification under strict text matching, yet functional analysis via the $n_{\text{necessary}}$ distribution revealed 0\% genuine in both cases (Table~\ref{tab:prolog-detailed}).
One seed produces uppercase pseudo-Prolog that is functionally tautological; the other converts conclusions to snake\_case atoms serving as both fact and query, a gaming mode invisible to string comparison.
Practitioners should cross-validate text-match classifiers with functional metrics and never treat classifier-reported genuine rates as ground truth without independent verification.

\paragraph{Practical guidelines.}
\label{app:practical-guidelines}
Our findings yield five guidelines for GRPO-trained neurosymbolic systems:
(1)~Never evaluate by prove rate alone; use ISR and component count as joint diagnostics.
(2)~Report multi-seed results: single-seed GRPO evaluation is unreliable, as cross-seed variance can exceed the effect size of interest (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
(3)~Use ISR for post-hoc diagnosis only, not as a training signal; any dose induces gaming or collapse.
(4)~Treat LOO-based metrics as component-count-biased until normalized.
(5)~Expect conclusion embedding as a GRPO-universal baseline (Table~\ref{tab:goodhart-landscape}): reward shaping alters hacking composition, not prevalence.

\paragraph{Multiple testing correction.}
\label{app:statistical-details}
We define two test families: FOLIO ($k{=}14$ tests across all conditions) and ProofFOL ($k{=}1$).
Within the FOLIO family, Bonferroni correction at $\alpha{=}0.05$ yields adjusted thresholds of $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.05/14{=}0.0036$.
Three primary comparisons survive correction: the TS rate difference (ISR vs.\ random; $p_{\text{bonf}}{=}1.82{\times}10^{-38}$), the SFT vs.\ exec-only non-hacking rate ($p_{\text{bonf}}{=}0.014$), and the Cochran--Mantel--Haenszel test for TS association across seeds ($p_{\text{bonf}}{<}10^{-8}$).
The matched 5+5-seed Fisher/Mann-Whitney comparison is borderline ($p_{\text{bonf}}{=}0.056$), significant at $\alpha{=}0.10$ after Bonferroni correction ($k{=}14$).
The ProofFOL genuine-rate permutation test ($p{=}0.10$) belongs to a separate hypothesis family (different dataset, independent experimental design) and does not reach significance even without correction; it is reported as an exploratory observation throughout.
Bonferroni assumes independence, which is conservative for our setting (several tests use overlapping data); Holm--Bonferroni or Benjamini--Hochberg FDR would recover the matched 5+5 comparison at conventional significance.
We report the most conservative Bonferroni results for transparency.


\section{Hacking Mode Definitions}
\label{app:hacking-modes}

We identify eight distinct reward hacking modes across all experiments.
Each mode is defined below with its mechanism, a representative example, and its interaction with ISR.
Table~\ref{tab:hacking-taxonomy-app} summarizes prevalence across FOL conditions.

\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}llcccc@{}}

\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
